samples.task_summary: Predict whether a BRFSS respondent has diabetes using health, behavior, and comorbidity features while favoring signals likely to generalize across domains.

scores.rationale: BMI is one of the strongest and most stable risk factors for diabetes across populations.
Underweight BMI category has limited direct relevance and is redundant with continuous BMI.
Normal-weight category is modestly informative as lower-risk reference but redundant with BMI.
Overweight status is a stable diabetes risk factor though less informative than obesity or continuous BMI.
Obesity is a strong, stable predictor of diabetes but partly redundant with continuous BMI.
Recent checkup can reflect diagnosis opportunity and healthcare access, making it somewhat predictive but potentially shortcut-like.
Checkup within past 2 years weakly reflects healthcare engagement rather than core disease biology.
Longer time since checkup is only weakly related and likely mediated by access and behavior.
Very infrequent checkups mostly encode healthcare access and ascertainment differences.
Never having a checkup is a brittle access-related signal with limited stable causal relevance.
Missingness here is likely survey/process related and not a stable semantic predictor.
Never having cholesterol checked mostly reflects healthcare access and screening patterns.
Recent cholesterol check may correlate with metabolic risk or diagnosis opportunity but is not a core stable signal.
Screening recency is weakly informative and partly reflects utilization differences.
Less recent cholesterol checks are mostly access-related with limited stable predictive value.
Missingness is likely process noise or subgroup eligibility rather than stable disease signal.
History of stroke is a stable comorbidity associated with vascular/metabolic disease burden.
Absence of stroke offers limited information beyond lack of comorbidity.
Missingness is unlikely to be a robust predictor.
Alcohol intake has a weak and potentially nonlinear association with diabetes risk, so only modest stable usefulness.
Very low education can proxy socioeconomic risk but is a demographic shortcut with domain sensitivity.
Low education is modestly predictive through socioeconomic pathways but not highly stable.
Some high school level modestly captures socioeconomic risk, though brittle across domains.
High school completion has weak predictive value through SES and health literacy.
Some college is only mildly informative and mostly socioeconomic.
College completion may inversely relate to diabetes risk but is a demographic shortcut more than direct biology.
Missing education is not a stable semantic predictor.
Frequent fruit consumption is a weak but plausible stable lifestyle correlate of lower diabetes risk.
Low fruit intake is modestly informative but self-report diet measures are noisy.
Diet missingness is mostly survey noise.
Having health coverage mainly captures access and eligibility rather than disease biology.
Lack of coverage may affect diagnosis opportunity and care access, making it brittle across domains.
This category mixes age eligibility and missingness, so it is not a clean stable predictor.
No high blood pressure is weakly informative as lower cardiometabolic risk.
Hypertension is a strong and stable comorbidity associated with diabetes and metabolic syndrome.
Missingness is not a robust semantic predictor.
Lowest income modestly captures socioeconomic risk but is a domain-sensitive shortcut.

Upper income category is only weakly informative and highly context dependent.
Low income is modestly predictive through access, diet, and environment but not robustly transportable.
Lower-middle income has similar modest SES signal.
Income categories in this range weakly proxy socioeconomic determinants of risk.
Mid income remains only modestly informative and not directly causal.
This income level has weak predictive value through SES patterns.
Higher income categories are weakly inversely associated with risk but brittle across domains.
High income is not a direct disease signal and may shift across settings.
Very high income has limited stable usefulness for OOD generalization.
Income missingness is process-related and unstable.
Survey year is a domain identifier and should be strongly penalized for OOD generalization.
Married status has weak indirect association via age and social factors, not stable disease biology.
Divorced status is only weakly informative and likely confounded.
Widowed status partly proxies older age and health burden but is a demographic shortcut.
Separated status has limited stable predictive value.
Never married status is weakly informative and mostly demographic.
Unmarried couple status has little stable relation to diabetes.
Missing marital status is not a robust predictor.
Cost barriers to care can correlate with poorer health and undermanaged risk, but mainly reflect access.
No cost barrier is only weakly informative.
Missingness is unstable and nonsemantic.
Poor mental health days have some association with chronic disease burden and self-care but are indirect.
Coronary heart disease/MI is a stable cardiometabolic comorbidity associated with diabetes.
Absence of CHD/MI provides limited information beyond lower comorbidity burden.
Missingness is not a stable predictor.
Poor physical health days reflect chronic disease burden and functional impact, moderately predictive though somewhat downstream.
Not binge drinking has weak relation to diabetes risk.
Binge drinking is only a weak and inconsistent predictor of diabetes.
Missingness is not semantically useful.
Sex has a real but moderate association with diabetes risk, though it is a sensitive demographic feature.
Daily smoking modestly relates to diabetes risk but less strongly than obesity or hypertension.
Some-day smoking is weakly predictive.
Not smoking currently is only mildly informative as lower-risk behavior.

Ever smoking 100 cigarettes captures lifetime smoking exposure with modest stable relevance.
Never smoker status is only weakly informative.
Missingness is not robustly predictive.
